body.text: On the sidelines of last month’s G20 summit in Atlanta, the top diplomats from Japan, South Korea, and the United States signed a memorandum of cooperation that seeks to extend their trilateral engagement into the Arctic.

This meeting marked the fourth time this year that Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio have met together, demonstrating the continuity of trilateral cooperation despite changes in government across all three capitals in 2025. With this memorandum, however, the parties have gone beyond maintaining existing arrangements and taken a new step into uncharted territory.

This raises two questions: Why the Arctic, and why now? After all, there is still considerable ground to cover in the current areas of trilateral cooperation, including North Korea and regional economic security across the Indo-Pacific corridor.

All three governments have independently recognized the mounting risks and opportunities in the Arctic. Their decision to collaborate trilaterally reflects a shared understanding that closer coordination will be necessary to navigate the region’s increasingly competitive strategic environment.

Although the full text of the new memorandum has not been published, it stands to provide a foundation for aligning the three countries’ economic and security interests in the Arctic, and could serve as a mechanism for deepening ties between the Northeast Asian partners.
Why the Arctic?

The Arctic is emerging as an increasingly important arena for strategic competition. The region is warming four times faster than any other area on Earth. This accelerated warming is contributing to the loss of sea ice, opening up new shipping lanes, and increasing access to previously inaccessible natural-resource deposits.

These physical changes have attracted significant commercial interest, particularly from natural resource extraction industries and the shipping sector. As this economic interest in the region has grown, so too have the political and security concerns across the Arctic.

One challenge for Tokyo, Seoul, and Washington is that all three countries are collectively behind in the race for Arctic capability and relevancy among Northeast Asian players. Russia currently holds the strongest position in the region, while China is working to expand its presence.

Russia’s Arctic advantage stems from its natural geography. It possesses the largest Arctic coastline of any country, and over half of Russia’s natural gas comes from its northern regions. Moscow also controls the Northern Sea Route (NSR) above the country’s northern coast, which benefits from being only two-thirds the length of the Suez route between East Asia and Europe.

Moscow is investing heavily in its Arctic regions, renovating former Soviet infrastructure and developing the Trans-Arctic Transportation Corridor (TATC). This project aims to connect ports and rail networks stretching from Vladivostok in the east to Murmansk in the west.

Meanwhile, China has sought to expand its Arctic presence. Leveraging its position as Russia’s largest and closest trading partner, Chinese state-owned enterprises have secured stakes in Russian energy projects while also investing in Russian Arctic infrastructure, including the development and modernization of ports in Russia’s Far East. At the same, shippers have sought to regularize transit using the NSR, with Chinese carrier Sea Legend recently launching its first routine container service on the route.

Japan and South Korea are non-Arctic states that have nevertheless maintained a stake in Arctic activities. Both countries have maintained observer status in the Arctic Council – the international body established to manage non-security issues related to the region – since 2013. Over the past decade, both Japan and South Korea have also demonstrated growing interest in the Arctic, with particular the commercial opportunities from emerging sea routes.

Although NATO members have expressed their concern and skepticism of Russia and the commercial viability of the NSR, several Asian governments have shown interest in Moscow’s ability to offer alternative shipping routes and energy supplies. This is particularly relevant for Japan and South Korea, whose energy supplies remain heavily dependent on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Approximately 90 percent of Japan’s crude oil imports and 70 percent of South Korea’s pass through the strait, leaving both countries exposed to disruptions along a critical maritime chokepoint.

Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has directed a revision of the country’s 2015 Arctic Policy, citing competition over resources and waterways. The revised strategy is expected to be published by spring 2027 and aims to raise Japan’s role in resource development and sea-route exploration. These ambitions will be supported by the country’s upcoming icebreaker, the Mirai II.

South Korea, meanwhile, has already begun translating its Arctic ambitions into commercial activity. Last month, the vessel PanStar Acro successfully returned from a trial commercial voyage from Busan to Gdansk and back via the NSR. President Lee Jae-myung described the route as an alternative option during times of crisis and has set a goal of establishing regular Arctic shipping services between Busan and Europe by 2030. The target forms part of a broader ambition to position Busan as a central node in Pacific shipping.

The United States stands apart from its partners in that it is an Arctic state, a member of the Arctic Council, and part of the NATO alliance – seven members of which are Arctic states. The Trump administration has clearly demonstrated its interests in expanding the U.S. role in the Arctic, most notably with its pursuit of Greenland, which resulted in a new agreement with Denmark and Greenland on future access and activities going forward.

Washington’s interests extend beyond Greenland. The United States has a direct stake in maintaining security across the Arctic and North Pacific, particularly as Russia continues to develop its military and economic infrastructure in the region and China expands its commercial presence. Bringing Japan and South Korea into a broader framework for Arctic cooperation could help Washington leverage their industrial and maritime capabilities while strengthening coordination among its Northeast Asian allies.
The Trilateral Arctic Pacific Partnership: What to Watch

The memorandum of cooperation brings these individual interests together under a new framework for trilateral engagement. Rather than pursuing their Arctic ambitions independently, Japan, South Korea, and the United States now have a mechanism through which they can coordinate their activities and explore opportunities for cooperation.

Although the full text of the memorandum has not been made public, Japan’s Foreign Ministry readout outlined two key elements. First, the three countries will establish the Trilateral Arctic Pacific Partnership (TAPP), which will include a trilateral Arctic working group.

Second, Japan’s readout mentioned two potential areas of cooperation: maritime cooperation, focusing on maritime safety and emergency response activities; and economic partnership, including information exchange and pursuit of potential commercial opportunities.

The limited detail could indicate either this is still an embryonic proposal or that the three governments are reluctant to disclose any details that could fuel competition with Russia and China. As such, it will be important to observe the concrete activities under the TAPP framework going forward.

This includes the potential for increased cooperation among the three countries’ militaries and coastguards in the North Pacific, potentially including joint patrols, maritime monitoring, and search-and-rescue exercises. Such activities could be particularly relevant in waters surrounding Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost island, and near the Bering Strait off Alaska.

Shipbuilding will be another area worth watching. Japan and South Korea both maintain strong shipbuilding industries, which could prove valuable as the parties seek to expand their Arctic presence. Doing so will require increased investment in shipbreakers and other vessels outfitted for passage through the region’s icy waters. Cooperation between the three governments could also create opportunities to align industrial capabilities, share technical expertise, and support the development of new vessels suited to Arctic operations.

Finally, the working group’s activities and the continued prominence of TAPP in high-level trilateral meetings will offer an indication of the initiative’s political importance going forward. The establishment of a working group is an important first step, but its effectiveness will depend on whether the three governments are willing to commit the necessary political attention and resources to turn the framework into practical cooperation.

Ultimately, the establishment of the Trilateral Arctic Pacific Partnership reflects a growing recognition in Tokyo, Seoul, and Washington that the Arctic is becoming an increasingly important arena for economic and strategic competition. Whether it develops into a meaningful pillar of trilateral cooperation is yet to be seen, but the parties have established the mechanism, should they choose to use it.
